title: Kubernetes Fundamentals
subtitle: Architecture, kubectl, Pods and cluster organization
description: Understand why Kubernetes exists, how its components fit together, and how to operate a cluster with kubectl, Pods, namespaces and labels.
outcomes: Explain control plane and node components
Work declaratively with kubectl and kubeconfig contexts
Run and debug Pods with probes and init containers
Organize workloads with namespaces and labels

modules.title: Architecture and kubectl
modules.summary: How a cluster is built and how you talk to it.

lessons.title: Why Kubernetes and its architecture
lessons.summary: What problem Kubernetes solves and how the control plane and worker nodes cooperate to run your workloads.
objectives: Explain what an orchestrator adds on top of a container runtime
Name every control plane and node component and its job
Trace what happens when a workload is submitted to the cluster

sections.title: From one container to a fleet
sections.body:
Running `docker run` on one host is easy. Running hundreds of containers across many machines is not: who restarts a crashed container, where does a new one fit, how do replicas find each other, how do you roll out a new version without downtime?

Kubernetes is a **container orchestrator**. You declare the **desired state** ("three replicas of this image, reachable on port 80") and the cluster continuously works to make reality match it. It provides scheduling, self-healing, service discovery, rolling updates and scaling as built-in primitives.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: Cluster components
head: Component
Where
Job
rows: The only front door: validates and stores objects, serves every client (kubectl, kubelet, controllers).
Consistent key-value store holding all cluster state. Only the API server talks to it.
Picks a node for each unscheduled Pod based on resources, affinity and taints.
Runs control loops (Deployment, Node, Job...) that drive actual state toward desired state.
Agent that starts the Pod's containers through the runtime and reports status.
Programs node networking rules so Service addresses reach the right Pods.
Actually runs containers, e.g. `containerd` or `CRI-O`, via the CRI interface.

sections.title: Everything goes through the API server
sections.body: Controllers, the scheduler and kubelets never talk to each other directly. They watch the API server for changes and write results back to it. That is why the API server and etcd are the heart of the cluster.

sections.title: What happens when you create a Deployment

items.title: kubectl sends the request
items.body: kubectl authenticates and POSTs the object to the API server, which validates it and persists it in etcd.

items.title: Controllers react
items.body: The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects with no node assigned.

items.title: Scheduler assigns nodes
items.body: The scheduler sees unscheduled Pods and binds each one to a suitable node.

items.title: Kubelet runs them
items.body: The kubelet on that node sees a Pod bound to it, asks the runtime to pull the image and start containers, and reports status back.

sections.body: These are three read-only kubectl commands that ask the API server about the cluster you are connected to. `kubectl get nodes -o wide` lists the machines, `get pods -n kube-system` lists the system Pods (the control plane parts from the table above), and `cluster-info` prints the API server address. We run them first because they confirm kubectl works and let you see the architecture for real. In the output, look at the ROLES column (control-plane versus worker) and the kube-apiserver, etcd and kube-scheduler Pods.

sections.code:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl cluster-info

sections.body: These commands ask the API server what it can do, instead of changing anything. `api-resources` lists every kind of object the cluster knows (Pod, Service, Deployment...), `api-versions` lists the group/version strings, and `/readyz?verbose` is a health check of the API server itself. You will need these names later when you write the `kind` and `apiVersion` lines of a manifest. In the output, look at the SHORTNAMES column (`po`, `svc`, `deploy`) and the NAMESPACED column.

kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | tail -4

lessons.title: kubectl, contexts and the declarative model
lessons.summary: Use kubectl to talk to clusters, manage kubeconfig contexts, and work declaratively with apply.
objectives: Switch between clusters and namespaces with contexts
Use apply, get, describe, logs and exec fluently
Contrast imperative commands with declarative manifests

sections.title: kubeconfig and contexts
sections.body:
`kubectl` reads `~/.kube/config` (or the files in `$KUBECONFIG`). It holds **clusters** (API server address and CA), **users** (credentials) and **contexts**, each pairing a cluster, a user and a default namespace.

The **current context** decides which cluster every command hits, so check it before anything destructive.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.body: These commands manage kubectl contexts, which are saved shortcuts to a cluster, a user and a namespace. `get-contexts` lists them, `current-context` shows the active one, `use-context` switches, and `set-context --current --namespace=...` changes the default namespace. We show them because working against the wrong cluster is a common mistake. In the output, the `*` marks the active context.

sections.code:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config use-context dev-cluster
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop
sections.title: Working with contexts
sections.output:
$ kubectl config get-contexts
CURRENT   NAME           CLUSTER        AUTHINFO      NAMESPACE
*         dev-cluster    dev-cluster    dev-admin     shop
          prod-cluster   prod-cluster   prod-reader

$ kubectl config current-context
dev-cluster

$ kubectl config use-context prod-cluster
Switched to context "prod-cluster".

$ kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop
Context "dev-cluster" modified.
sections.note: `use-context` rewrites `current-context` in the kubeconfig file. It is blocked in the app console, so run it in your own terminal; here, just read what it prints. The `*` marks the active context.

sections.body: This is an example `~/.kube/config`, the kubeconfig file kubectl reads on every command to learn which cluster to call and with which credentials. You do not apply it; you edit it indirectly with `kubectl config` commands or by pointing `KUBECONFIG` at it. The data here is fake. Look at the three lists `clusters`, `users` and `contexts`, and at `current-context`, which picks the active pair.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
current-context: dev-cluster          # context kubectl uses right now

clusters:                             # WHERE: API servers to talk to
  - name: dev-cluster
    cluster:
      server: https://127.0.0.1:6443
      certificate-authority-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...   # truncated CA cert (base64)
  - name: prod-cluster
    cluster:
      server: https://prod.example.com:6443
      certificate-authority-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...

users:                                # WHO: credentials
  - name: dev-admin
    user:
      client-certificate-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...
      client-key-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...
  - name: prod-reader
    user:
      token: <redacted>

contexts:                             # WHICH combination: cluster + user + default namespace
  - name: dev-cluster
    context:
      cluster: dev-cluster
      user: dev-admin
      namespace: shop
  - name: prod-cluster
    context:
      cluster: prod-cluster
      user: prod-reader
sections.title: ~/.kube/config (kubeconfig, fake data)
sections.note: `clusters` says where the API servers are and which CA to trust; `users` holds credentials (certificate pair, token or exec plugin); `contexts` pair one cluster with one user and an optional default namespace; `current-context` selects the active pair. Never commit or paste real kubeconfigs: they contain secrets. Use KUBECONFIG=a:b to merge several files. This is not a manifest, so it cannot be applied.

sections.title: Imperative versus declarative
sections.body: Imperative commands (`kubectl run`, `kubectl create`) tell the cluster what to do now. The declarative approach stores a manifest in Git and runs `kubectl apply -f`, which compares it with the live object and patches the difference. Re-running it is safe, which makes it the standard for real work.

`web-pod.yaml` is a manifest: a file that describes a Pod you want to exist. You pass it to `kubectl apply -f web-pod.yaml`, and kubectl sends it to the API server, which creates the object. It is the smallest useful example of the declarative style. Look at the four top-level keys `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` and `spec`, and in the spec the container name, image (`nginx:1.27`) and port.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
sections.title: web-pod.yaml
sections.note: Every object has apiVersion, kind, metadata and (usually) spec. The cluster fills in status.

sections.body: This is the everyday command sequence for the `web-pod.yaml` you just saw: create the Pod, check it, inspect it, read its logs, open a shell inside it and delete it. Each command is shown with realistic output so you know what success looks like. Look at STATUS `Running` in `get pod`, the Events at the bottom of `describe` (Scheduled, Pulled, Started) and the nginx startup lines in `logs`.

sections.code:
kubectl apply -f web-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod web -o wide
kubectl describe pod web
kubectl logs web
kubectl exec -it web -- sh
kubectl delete -f web-pod.yaml

sections.body: `web-deployment.yaml` is a manifest for a Deployment, the object you normally use instead of a bare Pod. You create it with `kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml`. Instead of one Pod, you declare the desired state (3 replicas) and a controller keeps it true. Look at `replicas: 3`, the `selector.matchLabels` that must match the labels in `template`, and the Pod template under `template.spec`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
sections.title: web-deployment.yaml (declarative desired state)
sections.note: You declare 3 replicas; the Deployment controller keeps 3 Pods alive and replaces any that disappear. Re-running `kubectl apply` after editing the file changes the cluster to match.

sections.body: These commands use `web-deployment.yaml` from above: `apply` creates or updates the Deployment, `get deployment` checks it, `diff` previews what an apply would change, and `get pod -o yaml` prints the full stored object. We show them to demonstrate the declarative loop and to reveal that the cluster adds fields you never wrote. In the output, look at READY `3/3`, the empty diff, and the `status` section at the end of the YAML.

sections.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get deployment web
kubectl diff -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get pod web -o yaml | head -20

sections.title: Preview before you change
sections.body: Use `kubectl diff -f file.yaml` to see what apply would change, and `--dry-run=client -o yaml` to generate a manifest skeleton without creating anything.

sections.title: Mind the current context
sections.body: Running `kubectl delete` against the wrong context is a classic outage. Show the context in your shell prompt or pass `--context` explicitly.

lessons.title: Pods in depth
lessons.summary: The Pod lifecycle, multi-container patterns, init containers, restart policy and basic probes.
objectives: Describe Pod phases and container states
Use init containers and understand restartPolicy
Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes

sections.title: The Pod is the unit of scheduling
sections.body: A **Pod** is one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, `localhost` between them) and can share volumes. All containers in a Pod land on the same node and live and die together. Pods are **ephemeral**: when one is deleted or its node fails, it is replaced by a new Pod with a new IP, which is why you rarely create bare Pods in production and use controllers like Deployments instead.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: Pod phases
head: Phase
Meaning
rows: Accepted, but not yet scheduled or images still pulling.
Bound to a node and at least one container is running or restarting.
All containers exited with code 0 and will not restart.
All containers terminated and at least one failed.

sections.title: Restart policy and init containers
sections.body:
`restartPolicy` (`Always` default, `OnFailure`, `Never`) controls whether the kubelet restarts containers that exit. Repeated crashes are delayed with exponential back-off, shown as `CrashLoopBackOff`.

**Init containers** run to completion one at a time before app containers start, useful for waiting on a dependency or preparing files.

This is `api-pod.yaml`, a manifest for a Pod that waits for its database before starting. You would create it with `kubectl apply -f api-pod.yaml`. It shows init containers and probes in a real shape. Look at `initContainers` (the `wait-db` loop that runs first), and under the main container the `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done']
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 8080
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 10
sections.title: Init container and probes
sections.note: `initContainers` run to completion one by one before the app starts. `readinessProbe` gates traffic; `livenessProbe` restarts a stuck container. `restartPolicy: Always` is the default for Pods that should keep running.

sections.body: This is `web-sidecar.yaml`, a manifest for a Pod with two containers that cooperate, applied with `kubectl apply -f web-sidecar.yaml`. It shows the sidecar pattern, shared storage, and resource settings in one file. Look at the `emptyDir` volume `logs` mounted by both containers, and the `resources.requests` and `limits` on the nginx container.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-sidecar
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 64Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 128Mi
      volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/nginx
    - name: log-tailer
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /logs/access.log']
      volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
  volumes:
    - name: logs
      emptyDir: {}
sections.title: Multi-container Pod with shared volume and resources
sections.note: Both containers share the Pod's network namespace (localhost) and the `emptyDir` volume `logs`, which lives as long as the Pod. `requests` are what the scheduler reserves; `limits` are the ceiling (exceed memory and the container is OOMKilled).

sections.title: Probes
head: Probe
Failure means
rows: App still starting; other probes are held off until it passes.
Container is stuck: the kubelet restarts it.
Not ready for traffic: removed from Service endpoints, not restarted.

sections.title: Do not make liveness depend on other services
sections.body: A liveness probe that checks the database will restart healthy app containers whenever the database blips. Keep liveness local to the process.

These are the commands you reach for when a Pod misbehaves, run here against the `api` Pod from the earlier manifest. `get pod -w` watches status changes live, `describe` shows state and Events, `logs --previous` shows the output of the last crashed container, and `jsonpath` extracts one field. In the output, look at the Init status moving to Running, the Restart Count, and the Warning events about the failed liveness probe.

sections.code:
kubectl get pod api -w
kubectl describe pod api
kubectl logs api -c api --previous
kubectl get pod api -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'

sections.body: This is sample output of `kubectl get pods` showing the STATUS values you will meet most often when something is wrong. It is not a file you create, just a reference to recognize problems. Compare the READY column (ready containers / total) and the STATUS names such as `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff`, `OOMKilled` and `Pending`, then read the note below for what each means.

sections.code:

web-sidecar     2/2     Running            0             5m
broken-image    0/1     ImagePullBackOff   0             2m
crashy          0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6 (40s ago)   8m
big-job         0/1     OOMKilled          3 (1m ago)    4m
pending-pod     0/1     Pending            0             6m
sections.title: Sample: common STATUS values in kubectl get pods
sections.note: READY is ready containers / total containers. `ImagePullBackOff`: wrong image name or no registry access. `CrashLoopBackOff`: the process keeps exiting, check `logs --previous`. `OOMKilled`: memory limit exceeded. `Pending`: not scheduled, check `describe` Events for insufficient resources or taints.

lessons.title: Namespaces, labels, selectors and annotations
lessons.summary: Organize and select objects with namespaces, labels and selectors, and attach metadata with annotations.
objectives: Label objects and query them with selectors
Know when to use annotations instead of labels

sections.title: Namespaces
sections.body: A **namespace** is a scope for names and for policy. Two teams can each have a Pod called `web` in different namespaces. Quotas, RBAC and network policies attach to namespaces. Default ones are `default`, `kube-system`, `kube-public` and `kube-node-lease`. Namespaces are not a hard security boundary on their own, and some objects (Nodes, PersistentVolumes) are cluster-scoped.

These commands create and use namespaces from the command line. `create namespace` makes a new scope, `-n staging` targets one namespace, `-A` lists across all of them, and `set-context --namespace` changes your default. We show them because most kubectl mistakes come from looking in the wrong namespace. In the output, look at the NAMESPACE column of `get pods -A`.

sections.code:
kubectl create namespace staging
kubectl get pods -n staging
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging
sections.title: Namespace commands
sections.output:
$ kubectl create namespace staging
namespace/staging created

$ kubectl get pods -n staging
No resources found in staging namespace.

$ kubectl get pods -A
NAMESPACE     NAME                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
default       web                         1/1     Running   0          6m
kube-system   coredns-7c65d6cfc9-4x2kq    1/1     Running   0          42d
kube-system   etcd-cp-1                   1/1     Running   0          42d
staging       web-1                       1/1     Running   0          2m

$ kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging
Context "dev-cluster" modified.

sections.body: `namespace.yaml` is the declarative way to create the same `staging` namespace: a manifest you apply with `kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml`. It is a good example of a minimal object with no `spec`. Look at `kind: Namespace`, the `name`, and the `env: staging` label under `metadata`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
sections.title: namespace.yaml
sections.note: A Namespace is just a named scope; names of namespaced objects only need to be unique inside it. Nodes and PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped and have no namespace.

sections.title: Labels and selectors
sections.body: **Labels** are key/value pairs on objects, used for identification and grouping. **Selectors** query them, and this is how Services find Pods and Deployments find their ReplicaSets. Labels are the glue of Kubernetes.

This is a Pod manifest, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, whose point is its `metadata`. It carries both labels and annotations, plus a namespace. Labels are used to select and group objects; annotations store extra information for humans and tools. Look at `labels` (app, tier, env) and `annotations` (owner, build-url).

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-1
  namespace: staging
  labels:
    app: web
    tier: frontend
    env: staging
  annotations:
    owner: team-shop@example.com
    build-url: https://ci.example.com/job/412
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27
sections.title: Labels and annotations

sections.body: These commands use labels to find and change objects. `-l` filters by a label selector (equality or `in (...)` sets), `--show-labels` prints every label, and `label` / `annotate` add metadata to an existing Pod. They show how you query a cluster by meaning, not by name. In the output, see which Pods each selector returns and the LABELS column.

sections.code:
kubectl get pods -l app=web
kubectl get pods -l 'env in (staging,prod),tier!=backend'
kubectl get pods --show-labels
kubectl label pod web-1 version=v2
kubectl annotate pod web-1 note='checked'
sections.title: Selecting and editing
sections.output:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web-1   1/1     Running   0          4m
web-2   1/1     Running   0          4m

$ kubectl get pods -l 'env in (staging,prod),tier!=backend'
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web-1   1/1     Running   0          4m

$ kubectl get pods --show-labels
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   LABELS
web-1   1/1     Running   0          4m    app=web,env=staging,tier=frontend
web-2   1/1     Running   0          4m    app=web,env=prod,tier=frontend
db-0    1/1     Running   0          4m    app=db,env=staging,tier=backend

$ kubectl label pod web-1 version=v2
pod/web-1 labeled

$ kubectl annotate pod web-1 note='checked'
pod/web-1 annotated
sections.note: Annotations hold non-identifying metadata (owners, URLs); labels are for selecting. Pods in `staging` can reach Services by short name inside the namespace and as `svc.staging` across namespaces.

sections.body: This is `web-service.yaml`, a manifest for a Service, applied with `kubectl apply -f web-service.yaml`. A Service gives a stable address to a changing set of Pods, and it finds them using labels. This shows selectors doing real work. Look at `spec.selector` (app and tier) and at `ports`, where `port` is what clients call and `targetPort` is the container's port.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: staging
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
    tier: frontend
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
sections.title: Selector in action: a Service
sections.note: The `selector` is the same label query as `-l app=web,tier=frontend`: any Pod in the namespace carrying both labels becomes an endpoint of this Service.

sections.body: These read-only commands check the result of the earlier steps: which namespaces exist, the details of `staging`, and which Pods the `web` Service actually selected. `get endpoints` is the quickest way to verify that a selector matches anything. In the output, look at the ENDPOINTS column, which lists the Pod IPs behind the Service.

sections.code:
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl describe namespace staging
kubectl get endpoints web -n staging

sections.title: Labels versus annotations
sections.body: Use labels for data you will select on. Annotations hold non-identifying metadata (URLs, owners, tool config) and cannot be used in selectors. Label values are limited to 63 characters.
